content: APRIL, also referred to as a proliferation-inducing ligand, is a protein that belongs to the tumor necrosis factor (TNF) ligand superfamily. It is also known by the designation TNFSF13. This protein interacts with the cell surface receptor TACI (transmembrane activator and CAML interactor). In the context of cluster of differentiation (CD) nomenclature, APRIL is identified as CD256. The protein encoded by the TNFSF13 gene is a member of the TNF ligand family. It serves as a ligand for TNFRSF17, also known as BCMA (B-cell maturation antigen), which is part of the TNF receptor family. Both APRIL and its receptor play a critical role in the development of B cells. Experimental studies conducted in vivo have demonstrated that APRIL is essential for the long-term survival of plasma cells within the bone marrow. However, mice that are deficient in APRIL exhibit normal immune system development. Despite this, APRIL-deficient mice have been observed to show a diminished capacity to support the survival of plasma cells. In vitro studies have suggested that APRIL may induce apoptosis through its interaction with other members of the TNF receptor family, such as TNFRSF6 (FAS) and TNFRSF14 (HVEM). Additionally, three alternatively spliced transcript variants of the TNFSF13 gene have been identified, each encoding distinct isoforms of the protein. APRIL has been shown to interact with TNFRSF13B (also known as TACI) and the B-cell activating factor (BAFF), further highlighting its role in B-cell biology. From a clinical perspective, APRIL is being investigated as a potential therapeutic target for autoimmune diseases and B-cell malignancies. At least one monoclonal antibody targeting APRIL has been announced to enter phase I clinical trials for the treatment of multiple myeloma.
